title: Differentiability Implies Continuity, Never the Reverse
quickIdea: f'(a) exists when the left and right difference quotients agree and are finite; that forces continuity at a, but continuity does not force a derivative.
remember: f'(a) = lim(h->0) (f(a + h) - f(a))/h, and the limit must be finite and two-sided.
Left derivative uses h -> 0- and right derivative uses h -> 0+; the derivative exists exactly when both exist and are equal.
Differentiable at a implies continuous at a. Proof idea: f(a + h) - f(a) = h * [(f(a + h) - f(a))/h], and the bracket is bounded near a.
Continuous at a does not imply differentiable: |x| at 0 is the standard counterexample.
Differentiability is a local statement - it says nothing about neighbouring points, and f' need not be continuous where it exists.
A vertical tangent (x^(1/3) at 0) is continuous but not differentiable: the difference quotient tends to infinity.

example.prompt: Show that f(x) = |x| is continuous but not differentiable at x = 0.
example.work: Continuity: for x > 0 f(x) = x -> 0, for x < 0 f(x) = -x -> 0, and f(0) = 0, so LHL = RHL = f(0). Derivatives: for h > 0 the quotient (|h| - 0)/h = 1; for h < 0 it is (-h)/h = -1. The two one-sided derivatives are 1 and -1.
example.answer: Continuous at 0 but not differentiable there, because the one-sided derivatives disagree. This is GATE CSE 1998 Q.1.4, whose answer is 'continuous but not differentiable'.

gateAngle: 1998 Q.1.4 asks exactly this pair of verdicts for |x| on [-1, 1]. 2024 Set 1 Q.1 asks for the set of points where max{x, x^3} fails to be differentiable, and 2025 Set 1 Q.21 makes differentiability at a join the condition that fixes a constant. The implication runs one way only, and every one of these questions depends on knowing that.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is f(x) = x|x| differentiable at x = 0?
variations.answer: Yes, with f'(0) = 0. For h > 0 the quotient is h^2/h = h -> 0, and for h < 0 it is -h^2/h = -h -> 0, so both one-sided derivatives are 0.
variations.why: The mirror image of |x|: the same piecewise structure, but the pieces meet with the same slope. It shows that a formula containing |x| is not automatically non-differentiable at the join.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does differentiability at a point force continuity there?
variations.answer: Because f(a + h) - f(a) = h * [(f(a + h) - f(a))/h], and as h -> 0 the first factor tends to 0 while the bracket tends to the finite number f'(a); the product tends to 0, which is exactly lim f(a + h) = f(a).
variations.why: The proof is one line and it explains why the converse cannot hold: the argument needs the bracket to have a limit, and continuity gives no such thing.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Is f(x) = x^(2/3) differentiable at x = 0?
variations.answer: No. It is continuous at 0, but the difference quotient is h^(2/3)/h = h^(-1/3), which tends to +infinity from the right and -infinity from the left - a cusp, not a finite derivative.
variations.why: A third way to fail: not a corner with two finite slopes, but a cusp where the slopes are infinite. GATE has used max and min functions to build such points.

trap.what: Assuming that a continuous function is differentiable, and checking differentiability by comparing formulas on the two pieces only.
trap.why: Continuity constrains values, differentiability constrains slopes; the second is strictly stronger. And matching the two formulas' slopes is not enough - the difference quotient itself must have a two-sided limit at the join.
trap.counterexample: |x| is continuous at 0 and has no derivative there. max{x, x^3} is continuous everywhere yet not differentiable at -1, 0 and 1.

check.question: Is f(x) = |x - 2| differentiable at x = 2?
check.explanation: It is continuous at 2, but the one-sided derivatives are -1 and 1. A shift of |x| fails at the point where its argument vanishes.
